# Blog voice

How posts under `src/content/blog/` should read. Reference example: `shopifys-aquifer-in-the-open.mdx`.

The target is the voice of Shopify's "Under the River" engineering post, written in first person. Confident, plain, technical without posturing. Sounds like an engineer explaining a real opinion to peers, not a marketing page and not an essay.

## Do

- **Open with an opinion, not a summary.** Take a position in the first two paragraphs. Disagree with something. If the post only restates a source, it has no reason to exist.
- **Short declarative sentences, varied with longer ones.** Let a fragment land for emphasis: "That is the easy version." "A product does."
- **Repeat the key noun** instead of reaching for synonyms. "The corpus", "the memory", "the session". Repetition builds the through-line.
- **Open each section with a constraint or fact, then pivot to the insight.**
- **First person.** "We made the same bet." "I wrote about that split in..." Own the claim.
- **Argue with specifics.** Name the table, the mechanism, the real difference. Vague beats nothing, specific beats vague.
- **Plain, slightly declarative headers.** Statements or mild antithesis: "The corpus is the asset. The conversation isn't." Not clever, not cute.

## Don't

- **No em dashes.** Hard rule for all landing copy. Use periods, commas, or parentheses. This also forces the staccato rhythm we want.
- **No three-beat marketing chants.** "Your agent. Your data. Your servers." is the single clearest AI tell. Kill it on sight.
- **No rhetorical questions** as a transition ("So why store the noise?").
- **No stacked tricolons** or relentless "not X, but Y" balance in every paragraph. One antithesis per stretch, not five.
- **No clever-for-clever's-sake** word pairs ("noise vs signal", "same goal, different cut", "strictly harder"). They read as filler.
- **No hedging AI filler:** "it's worth noting", "on one hand / on the other", "in today's world".
- **Don't paraphrase the source** section by section. Engage two or three points with depth instead of touring all of them.

## Shape

- Comparison or opinion posts: roughly 600 to 700 words.
- 3 to 5 sentences per paragraph, rarely longer.
- Quote a source verbatim when it sharpens the point, but keep quotes short.

## The test

Read it out loud. If a line sounds like a slide deck or a press release, rewrite it. If it sounds like you talking, keep it.

1	---
2	title: "Self-Improving Agents Are Event-Sourced"
3	description: "Keeping the record is the precondition for an agent improving. Append-only events, a delete-blocking trigger, entities derived from the log, and approvals recorded as supersession."
4	date: 2026-07-28
5	author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
6	authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
7	tags: [architecture, agents, memory, event-sourcing]
8	cover: /design/prim-events.webp
9	draft: false
10	---
11	
12	import { TruthProxyDiagram } from "../../components/blog/TruthProxyDiagram";
13	
14	Most of the proposals I see for self-improving agents are model-side. Yohei Nakajima's [survey of the field](https://yoheinakajima.com/better-ways-to-build-self-improving-ai-agents/) is a good map of them: reflection loops, self-correction training, self-generated curricula, agents that rewrite their own code. I've come round to a more boring position, and I want to state it narrowly, because the loose version of this claim is wrong.
15	
16	You can improve an agent by retraining it, or by rewriting its instructions, and neither needs a log. But every one of those routes needs a record of what the agent did, what a human said about it, and what happened afterwards, and that record is a storage problem. Event sourcing solved it a decade before anyone was building agents. Storage is not the improvement. It is what the improvement is computed from, and it is the part most teams skip while arguing about the mechanism on top.
17	
18	That storage can't be another system of record. The truth already has homes. Slack owns the conversation, Stripe owns the payment, the warehouse owns revenue, and moving them means owning a reconciliation problem you did not have before. So the log we built for Lobu is a proxy: an append-only record of observations about systems we don't own. The sources stay authoritative for the underlying facts. The log is authoritative for what we observed, when, and what every agent did about it.
19	
20	<TruthProxyDiagram />
21	
22	## The database refuses to forget
23	
24	Every row is an observation: a Slack thread a feed pulled, a payment webhook, a note an agent saved. Changing a fact means appending a new row that points at the one it replaces, via `supersedes_event_id`. There is no UPDATE path and no DELETE path.
25	
26	Current state is therefore derived rather than authoritative. The read view is where it comes from, and the whole mechanism is one `NOT EXISTS`:
27	
28	```sql
29	WHERE NOT EXISTS (
30	  SELECT 1 FROM public.events newer
31	  WHERE newer.supersedes_event_id = e.id
32	)
33	```
34	
35	A row is current if nothing supersedes it. The domain objects are the projection over that: a company, a member, a deal, each assembled from the events that mention it, with the derivation recorded down to the `sourceEventId` that produced a given relationship. Ask why an entity says what it says and the answer is a list of observations, not a row somebody edited.
36	
37	We tried putting a faster projection underneath that and it didn't earn its place. For one day in June there was a trigger-maintained table holding the latest value of every entity field, fed by a producer that emitted an event per changed field. The comment on the table demoted it exactly the way you'd hope, calling itself a rebuildable cache and naming the log as the source of truth. Then we dropped it, because nothing ever read it: entity metadata still came from the entity row, so the whole apparatus was overhead on the hot write path. The events it emitted are still in the log, harmless, because the log is never rewritten.
38	
39	That is the part I'd keep. Deleting a projection cost us a migration and nothing else, and the events that fed it are still sitting there if we ever want it back. When the log is the source of truth, a cache is a guess you're allowed to be wrong about.
40	
41	![Loose event cards on a conveyor, three bundles of them converging into three layered blocks on a workbench, and a reviewer stamping a card that returns on the rail below](/blog/entity-projection.webp)
42	
43	The append-only rule was a convention for a long time, written in a `COMMENT ON TABLE` and in our AGENTS.md, and not enforced at the database boundary at all. Any psql session or admin tool could still wipe rows. So it became a trigger:
44	
45	```sql
46	CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.events_block_direct_delete()
47	  RETURNS trigger AS $$
48	BEGIN
49	  IF pg_trigger_depth() > 1 THEN
50	    RETURN OLD; -- FK cascade (org delete) or another trigger's cleanup
51	  END IF;
52	  IF current_setting('lobu.allow_event_delete', true) = 'on' THEN
53	    RETURN OLD; -- sanctioned maintenance, transaction-scoped
54	  END IF;
55	  RAISE EXCEPTION
56	    'events is append-only: DELETE of event % blocked.',
57	    OLD.id
58	    USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation';
59	END;
60	$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
61	```
62	
63	The escape hatches are the interesting part. Deleting an organization genuinely does need to sweep its events, so cascades pass through at trigger depth greater than one. Sanctioned maintenance opts in explicitly, and it uses `SET LOCAL` so the bypass does not persist beyond the transaction that asked for it. This stops accidents, not a determined operator with database access. An escape hatch that outlives its transaction isn't an escape hatch.
64	
65	As of July 2026, 27,108 of the 224,420 rows in our log supersede an earlier observation. You keep every version rather than overwriting, and most of them nobody will ever read. That sounds wasteful right up until the first time somebody asks what the agent believed on Tuesday.
66	
67	## Session logs make the same trade
68	
69	Lobu's agent runtime is [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi), Mario Zechner's coding-agent harness, and a pi session is an append-only JSONL file. User turn, assistant turn, tool result, one entry after another, never edited in place. Replaying it reconstructs the transcript and the recorded tool results, which is enough to resume. It does not re-derive the model's output or the state of anything the tools touched.
70	
71	I don't think that's a coincidence. The good coding agents converged on append-only session files because it's what makes a run resumable and auditable, and those two properties are most of what makes the harness feel reliable.
72	
73	So Lobu runs the same shape one level up. Instead of one file per session, the organization gets one log, and the session meets it everywhere: a Behavior fires and the triggering event arrives in the session as a message, the agent asks for more context and events come back as tool results, and everything the agent does flows back into the log stamped with the run that did it.
74	
75	The part I didn't anticipate is how much of multi-agent coordination this covers. Two agents cooperate the same way two services in any event-sourced system do: one writes, the other reacts, and neither needs to know the other exists. We never built a multi-agent feature. What a shared log does not give you is ordering guarantees, idempotency, or any answer to two agents deciding the same thing at once, and those are still ours to handle.
76	
77	We are not the only ones landing here. Nakajima's [ActiveGraph](https://github.com/yoheinakajima/activegraph) is an event-sourced runtime for agents built on the same principle, where the working graph is a projection of the log and every mutation is an event. Its best trick is fork-and-diff: branch a run at any historical event, configure the fork differently, and structurally diff the result against the parent, with the shared prefix replaying from cache so the branch costs no new model calls.
78	
79	The difference is what the log is holding. ActiveGraph is a runtime for agent runs, and its README says plainly that it is not a production graph database. Forking a run makes sense there, because a run is a self-contained thing you can re-execute. Our events come from Slack, Gmail, GitHub, Linear, Stripe webhooks, and two dozen other systems we don't own, and the actions go back out to them. You cannot fork sending the email. The interesting replays for us are not counterfactual runs but real consequences arriving late: the reply that came back, the payment that failed, the human who edited the arguments before approving.
80	
81	That is also why we record replacement relationships between events rather than treating each one as independent. Treating every event as standalone is simpler and I would pick it for a run-local trace. We need supersession because a fact we mirrored can change underneath us, and the honest record of that is a new observation pointing at the old one, not a rewritten row.
82	
83	## Approvals use the same event model
84	
85	The place this paid off most is the bit every agent platform ends up bolting on: human approval for consequential writes.
86	
87	Ours is the same log. When an agent wants to do something gated, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. Approving doesn't update that event, it appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with whoever decided. The action's outcome supersedes again later, carrying the output or the error.
88	
89	What makes that card an actual interface is the envelope on the event. Alongside the proposed input, the event carries the JSON schema describing that input. The web app feeds the schema into a form, so the reviewer can edit the arguments before approving rather than voting yes or no on someone else's draft. The same event renders as a Slack card with buttons, and both paths call the same tool underneath. The UI is a function of the event, which is why a new interaction type doesn't need a new screen.
90	
91	The envelope is a wire contract rather than a convention, and it became one the hard way: the fields were scattered string literals across the MCP plugin, the server tools, and the web app, so the watcher-to-behavior rename broke card routing on one side while the other kept emitting the old word. Now the emitters import the same constants, the schemas derive from them, and a parity test fails if the app's accepted values drift from the contract.
92	
93	The table currently permits three interaction types: `none`, `approval` for a gated write, and `suggestion` for something the agent offers without blocking on it. That's a smaller vocabulary than I expected we'd need.
94	
95	Two consequences I'd flag. The worker's claim query only ever selects approved work, so an unapproved action isn't blocked by a check that someone has to remember to write; the normal claim path cannot select it at all. And approvals nobody decides expire after seven days, with expired kept as a status distinct from rejected, because an agent should never get to learn that silence means disapproval.
96	
97	## Why this is the improvement
98	
99	Every action lands in the log with run provenance. The outcome lands later as more events. The approvals, the rejections, the edited inputs, the guidance an admin writes: all of it lands too, attributed and permanent, and the next run reads it.
100	
101	None of that is clever, which is the part I'd defend. The model in the loop gets better a few times a year, when a lab ships something. The record underneath gets better every week, and what you do with it, whether that is retrieval, a rewritten prompt, or an eval set, is a separate problem you now have the inputs for. I'd rather own the second one.
102	
103	## Notifications are a query, not a firehose
104	
105	The last piece falls out of the same shape. Once every consequential thing is an event with an envelope, notifying a human is a selection over the log rather than a separate delivery system. An agent calls `notify`, the recipients resolve to members, and the notification is itself recorded, so what got surfaced to whom is as inspectable as everything else.
106	
107	This is the part I'd be careful with, and I mean careful in the product sense rather than the engineering sense. A system that knows what you approved, what you ignored until it expired, and what you edited before letting through has everything it needs to get very good at pulling your attention. The same feedback that makes the agent more useful makes it better at interrupting you. Optimizing engagement on that substrate would work, which is exactly why it's the wrong objective to point it at.
108	
109	The one guardrail I'll defend is the one already in the approvals path: expired is a distinct status from rejected, and nothing escalates on silence. An agent should learn from the decisions you actually made, not from how many times it managed to make you look.
110	
111	Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.
112

--
-- Behaviors authored with no sources persist a default all-events source

-- insertEvent stamps occurred_at, an unchanged default source would let a

---
title: Memory
description: Why Lobu uses entity-based memory instead of flat per-user files, and how a single fact becomes shared organizational context.
---

import { EntityMemoryDiagram } from "../../../components/blog/EntityMemoryDiagram";
import { BehaviorTraceCard } from "../../../components/memory/BehaviorTraceCard";

Most agent memory systems are flat files scoped to one user. The agent appends notes, then re-scans them every turn to recall context. That works for a personal assistant. It breaks the moment two agents — or a behavior, or another teammate — need to converge on the same fact.

Lobu's memory layer is **entity-based**: facts attach to typed entities (Company, Project, Member), so any agent in your org reads the same record.

## Filesystem vs entity memory

This is the same split data teams already use. Analysts pull data into a notebook, run scripts, produce charts — then write the durable result back to the warehouse so the rest of the business can use it. Nobody asks an analyst to do every query in production tables, and nobody runs the company off one analyst's notebook.

Agents need both layers too:

- **Filesystem** is the agent's notebook — ephemeral. Downloaded PDFs, scratch scripts, intermediate CSVs, generated reports. One agent, one channel, one task.
- **Entity memory** is the warehouse — durable. Customer facts, decisions, project state, recurring operational knowledge. Shared across agents, sessions, and operators.

A note on a Slack DM filesystem dies with the sandbox. A fact written to `Company:Acme` survives and shows up the next time *any* agent — billing, support, CSM — touches Acme.

For the longer argument and where to draw the line between the two, see [Filesystem vs Database for Agent Memory](/blog/filesystem-vs-database-agent-memory/).

## Entity memory in practice

A single inbound fact lands on the right entity and accumulates alongside everything else known about that customer:

<EntityMemoryDiagram
  prompt="Acme's CTO left in March, no exec champion since"
  rootLabel="Company"
  rootEmoji="🏢"
  entities={[
    { label: "Globex", emoji: "🏢" },
    {
      label: "Acme",
      emoji: "🏢",
      target: true,
      items: [
        { emoji: "🧑‍💼", text: "CTO departed 2026-03 — no exec champion" },
        { emoji: "🐞", text: "Behavior: 3 open Linear bugs this week" },
        { emoji: "📉", text: "DSCR 1.1× (Q1 review)" },
        { emoji: "🗓️", text: "Renewal due May 2026" },
        { emoji: "✅", text: "Decision: declined $2M extension — DSCR below 1.2×" },
      ],
    },
    { label: "Initech", emoji: "🏢" },
  ]}
/>

Different sources, same destination. A CSM's note in Slack, a behavior ingesting Linear bugs, and a credit decision from a separate agent all converge on `Company:Acme`. The next agent that reads Acme — through search, recall, or an explicit lookup — sees the full picture without re-deriving it from scratch.

This is the moat: shared, queryable, operator-visible memory that survives the sandbox.

## Behaviors

You don't sit at your desk thinking about every Slack message — but at night your brain replays the day, drops the noise, and consolidates what mattered into long-term memory. That's what behaviors do for your agent.

A behavior has three pieces: a **trigger** (a schedule, or a connector event, that wakes it), a **prompt** (what to remember and what to ignore), and an **entity** to attach memory to. The prompt is the filter — it tells the agent which signals from a noisy event stream actually matter, so it doesn't write down every OOO message and lunch plan.
=========== BEHAVIORS ===========
---
title: Behaviors
description: A behavior is a standing goal that watches your events and acts. It is the unit of business logic you own instead of renting from a vertical SaaS.
---

A behavior is the part of a vertical SaaS tool you used to buy, built once and owned. It is a standing goal — written once in config, applied to every matching event, and run on a schedule you control. Connectors feed events into the log; a behavior reads the new ones, decides what matters, and acts: remember, notify, request approval, or write back to the world.

You are not scripting the steps. You say what to watch for, which agent runs it, what it should remember, and where it should stop and ask a human. Lobu runs the rest of the loop.

## The anatomy of a behavior

A behavior has five moving parts:

- **Agent** — every behavior belongs to exactly one agent. The agent carries the persona, skills, tools, providers, and guardrails the behavior runs with.
- **Trigger** — what wakes it. A schedule (cron), a connector event, or both. The trigger says *when*, never *what*.
- **Prompt** — the goal, written once. A Handlebars template rendered with the window's entities, content, and SQL sources. The prompt is the filter: it tells the agent which signals from a noisy stream actually matter.
- **Sources** *(optional)* — named SQL queries against the events log, bound into the prompt. This is how a behavior reads the data a connector wrote.
- **Reaction** *(optional)* — a typed TypeScript script that runs after extraction, where the behavior actually acts: post to Slack, write a derived event, call an external API. See [Reactions](/sdks/reactions/).

## Define one

Behaviors live in `lobu.config.ts`, declared at the project level and owned by an agent via `defineBehavior`:

```ts
import { defineConfig, defineBehavior, reactionFromFile } from "@lobu/cli/config";

const reconciliationMonitor = defineBehavior({
  agent: finance, // owning agent (handle or id)
  slug: "reconciliation-monitor", // stable diff key
  name: "Reconciliation monitor",
  triggers: [{ kind: "schedule", cron: "0 6 * * 1-5" }], // weekdays, 6am
  notification: { priority: "high", channel: "both" },
  tags: ["finance", "reconciliation", "daily"],
  minCooldownSeconds: 3600, // never fire more than once an hour
  reaction: reactionFromFile("./reconciliation-monitor.reaction.ts"),
  prompt:
    "Check accounts for unreconciled transactions, new variances, and approaching reporting deadlines. Lead with exceptions that need review.",
});
```

`lobu apply` diffs this against the org's current state and reconciles — a behavior is versioned config, not a script you deploy by hand.

## Reading events with sources

A behavior with no sources only sees the event window that triggered it. To reason over history — the last 200 Gmail messages, this week's Stripe charges, a customer's full timeline — add named SQL sources. Each source is a query against the append-only events log, and its result is bound into the prompt by name:

---
title: "Self-Improving Agents Are Event-Sourced"
description: "An agent improves when its past is queryable. How Lobu's memory writes, feed ingestion, Behaviors, and approval gates are all the same append-only log, and where the git analogy stops."
date: 2026-07-28
author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
tags: [architecture, agents, memory, event-sourcing]
cover: /design/prim-events.webp
draft: false

import { TruthProxyDiagram } from "../../components/blog/TruthProxyDiagram";

An agent gets better when its past is queryable. Most of what gets proposed for self-improving agents is model-side: reflection loops, self-generated curricula, agents that rewrite their own prompts. Every one of those needs the same input, which is an honest record of what the agent did, what a human said about it, and what happened afterwards. That is a storage problem, and it was solved a decade before anyone shipped an agent.

So Lobu is closer to git than to a memory API. Every write is an append. Nothing is edited in place. Correcting a fact means writing a new one that points at the fact it replaces. History is walkable, provenance is a column, and human review is a merge step that happens before the write lands rather than a cleanup afterwards.

The log is not another system of record. Slack owns the conversation, Stripe owns the payment, the warehouse owns revenue, and mirroring them into a second authority buys you a reconciliation problem you did not have. Our log is a proxy: an append-only record of observations about systems we do not own. The sources stay authoritative for the facts. The log is authoritative for what we observed, when, and what every agent did about it.

<TruthProxyDiagram />

## A memory write is a commit

The agent-facing surface is one MCP tool, `save_memory`, and its contract is the whole model in a sentence: storage is append-only, pass `supersedes_event_id` to replace an existing fact, and the old event is hidden from future searches without losing history.

Agents are told to use it that way. The guidance we ship reads: "When a message changes a fact you already stored (an updated preference, status, count, location, or plan), first search for the prior memory to get its id, then save the new value with `supersedes_event_id` set to that id."

The chain is enforced, not conventional. A partial unique index means at most one event can supersede a given target, so the loser of a concurrent-supersede race gets a `23505` and a real error instead of a fork. Current state is a view over that: an event is current if nothing supersedes it. Read a fact's history and the server walks the `supersedes_event_id` linked list in both directions and hands back every version.

In our own workspace that is 229,377 events, of which 27,198 replace an earlier observation. You keep every version, and most of them nobody will ever read. That sounds wasteful right up until somebody asks what the agent believed on Tuesday.

## Ingestion is incremental by construction

Facts arrive through feeds. A feed is one connector-defined sync against one connection, and it carries a `checkpoint` that the connector advances itself, so the next run pulls from where the last one stopped rather than re-reading the source.

Duplicates are handled at the insert, not by the connector. Ingest dedupes on `(connection_id, origin_id)` under a per-item advisory lock, so two concurrent syncs of the same Slack thread serialize on that item and different items never contend. Re-running a sync is cheap and safe, which is the property that lets a connector be dumb.

Behaviors get incrementality from the log itself. A Behavior's unprocessed work is computed as a diff: total events per month, minus events already linked to one of that Behavior's completed windows. There is no cursor to corrupt and no watermark to reset. If a window fails, its events are simply still unlinked, so the next run picks them up.

## Behaviors write back into the graph

A Behavior is a trigger, a prompt, and optional named SQL sources over the events log. The trigger says when. The prompt says what matters. The sources are how it reads the data a connector wrote. When it runs, it completes a window, and the window records exactly which events it consumed.

What it produces goes back into the same graph in one of two shapes. It appends events, which is a memory, a summary, a notification, an approval request. Or it changes entities, which is the structured layer: a company's stage, a member's role, a deal's amount.

That loop needs one guard, and we learned it the mechanical way. Behaviors with no explicit source used to read every event. The server's own bookkeeping rows, `semantic_type` of `change` and `audit`, were invisible only by accident, because they were inserted with a null `occurred_at`. The moment we started stamping that column, a Behavior's own audit trail became new workspace content it would react to. The default source now excludes those two semantic types, and a migration rewrote the existing rows matched by exact literal so hand-authored sources were never touched.

![Loose event cards on a conveyor, three bundles of them converging into three layered blocks on a workbench, and a reviewer stamping a card that returns on the rail below](/blog/entity-projection.webp)

## The human review step is a merge

Entity fields carry ownership. `entities.field_controls` is a sparse map where a key being present means a human owns that field. There is one write path for both humans and agents, and it behaves differently by source: a human write sets the value and marks it owned, and an agent write only lands on fields no human has claimed.

Blocked fields do not fail silently and they do not overwrite. Every user-facing entity mutation runs through a gate that can allow, deny, or defer, and a deferred write becomes a pending run plus an approval event, queued strictly after the caller's transaction commits so approvals never ride a write that might roll back.

The approval event is what makes this collaboration rather than a yes/no vote. Alongside the proposed input, the event carries the JSON schema describing that input, so the web app renders a form and the reviewer edits the arguments before approving. One run that proposed twenty field changes groups into one card through its window id. The same event renders as a Slack card with buttons, and both paths call the same tool underneath.

## Every row names the run that wrote it

This is the part that turns a log into an audit trail. Events carry `run_id`, and a run carries the Behavior that fired it, the agent that Behavior belongs to, and the user who initiated it if a human did. 90,990 of our 229,377 events name their run.

That gives a run transaction-like handles after the fact. The writes from one Behavior execution are a set you can select, review as a batch, attribute to an agent, and supersede as a batch. "Why does this company say Series B" resolves to a run, a window, the events that window consumed, and the human who approved the promotion.

## Where the analogy stops

There is no force-push and no rebase, because a fact we mirrored can change under us and the honest record of that is a new observation pointing at the old one. There is no revert either. You cannot un-send the email. That asymmetry is the reason the gate sits before the write and the correction is an append.

None of this is clever, which is the part I would defend. The model in the loop gets better a few times a year when a lab ships something. The record underneath gets better every week, and what you do with it, whether that is retrieval, a rewritten prompt, or an eval set, is a separate problem you now have the inputs for.

Start with the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/), or read how [Behaviors](/getting-started/behaviors/) are defined.

That is an analyst working on one laptop. It works at one desk, and nobody runs a company off it.

I have argued that analogy in full in [The Modern Data Stack for Agents](/blog/the-modern-data-stack-for-agents/), and the split between the notebook and the warehouse in [Filesystem vs Database for Agent Memory](/blog/filesystem-vs-database-agent-memory/). The log is authoritative for what we observed, when, and what every agent did about it.

<TruthProxyDiagram />

## A memory write is a commit

The agent-facing surface is one MCP tool, `save_memory`, and its contract is the whole model in a sentence: storage is append-only, pass `supersedes_event_id` to replace an existing fact, and the old event is hidden from future searches without losing history.

Agents are told to use it that way. The guidance we ship reads: "When a message changes a fact you already stored (an updated preference, status, count, location, or plan), first search for the prior memory to get its id, then save the new value with `supersedes_event_id` set to that id."

The chain is enforced, not conventional. A partial unique index means at most one event can supersede a given target, so the loser of a concurrent-supersede race gets a `23505` and a real error instead of a fork. Current state is a view over that: an event is current if nothing supersedes it. Read a fact's history and the server walks the `supersedes_event_id` linked list in both directions and hands back every version.

In our own workspace that is 229,377 events, of which 27,198 replace an earlier observation. You keep every version, and most of them nobody will ever read. That sounds wasteful right up until somebody asks what the agent believed on Tuesday.

## Ingestion is incremental by construction

Facts arrive through feeds. A feed is one connector-defined sync against one connection, and it carries a `checkpoint` that the connector advances itself, so the next run pulls from where the last one stopped rather than re-reading the source.

Duplicates are handled at the insert, not by the connector. Ingest dedupes on `(connection_id, origin_id)` under a per-item advisory lock, so two concurrent syncs of the same Slack thread serialize on that item and different items never contend. Re-running a sync is cheap and safe, which is the property that lets a connector be dumb.

Behaviors get incrementality from the log itself. A Behavior's unprocessed work is computed as a diff: total events per month, minus events already linked to one of that Behavior's completed windows. There is no cursor to corrupt and no watermark to reset. If a window fails, its events are simply still unlinked, so the next run picks them up.

## Behaviors are mutations on your data model

A Behavior is a trigger, a prompt, and optional named SQL sources over the events log. The trigger says when. The prompt says what matters. The sources are how it reads what a connector wrote. It subscribes to company events, and when it runs it completes a window that records exactly which events it consumed.

What it produces goes back into the same graph in one of two shapes. It appends events, which is a memory, a summary, a notification, an approval request. Or it changes entities, which is the structured layer: a company's stage, a member's role, a deal's amount. That is the whole vocabulary. A Behavior is a mutation against your data model with a model in the middle deciding the arguments.

That loop needs one guard, and we learned it the mechanical way. Behaviors with no explicit source used to read every event. The server's own bookkeeping rows, `semantic_type` of `change` and `audit`, were invisible only by accident, because they were inserted with a null `occurred_at`. The moment we started stamping that column, a Behavior's own audit trail became new workspace content it would react to. The default source now excludes those two semantic types, and a migration rewrote the existing rows matched by exact literal so hand-authored sources were never touched.

![Loose event cards on a conveyor, three bundles of them converging into three layered blocks on a workbench, and a reviewer stamping a card that returns on the rail below](/blog/entity-projection.webp)

## The human review step is a merge

Entity fields carry ownership. `entities.field_controls` is a sparse map where a key being present means a human owns that field. There is one write path for both humans and agents, and it behaves differently by source: a human write sets the value and marks it owned, and an agent write only lands on fields no human has claimed.

Blocked fields do not fail silently and they do not overwrite. Every user-facing entity mutation runs through a gate that can allow, deny, or defer, and a deferred write becomes a pending run plus an approval event, queued strictly after the caller's transaction commits so approvals never ride a write that might roll back.

The approval event is what makes this collaboration rather than a yes/no vote. Alongside the proposed input, the event carries the JSON schema describing that input, so the web app renders a form and the reviewer edits the arguments before approving. One run that proposed twenty field changes groups into one card through its window id. The same event renders as a Slack card with buttons, and both paths call the same tool underneath.

Rejection is not a dead end either. A correction a human makes on a Behavior's output is itself an event, `semantic_type` of `correction`, and the next run of that Behavior gets the most recent correction per field folded into its prompt. Superseded corrections are dropped so the prompt does not accumulate the whole argument. The human is editing the agent's future behaviour by editing the record, which is the only feedback channel we have that survives a model swap.

## Every run writes to the same log

Agents still get a filesystem. Each conversation gets a workspace for the scratch work: downloaded PDFs, intermediate CSVs, generated reports. That layer stays ephemeral on purpose. What leaves it is the write to the log, and every one of those names the run that made it. A run carries the Behavior that fired it, the agent that Behavior belongs to, and the user who initiated it if a human did. 90,990 of our 229,377 events name their run.

The same is true of agents we do not run. Connect ChatGPT to the Lobu MCP server and every tool call it makes writes an audit event carrying the agent id, the MCP session, the client, and the calling user, alongside the tool name, a hash of the arguments, and a redacted preview. The audit records the call's shape, never its content, and credentials are consumed to the end of the value rather than to the first space. On Slack, a thread is a conversation in its own right, keyed as `slack:{channel}:{thread}` and pinned to one agent, so a thread is a durable run rather than a session that dies with the socket.

That is what gives you one audit trail across managed and external agents instead of one per vendor. "Why does this company say Series B" resolves to a run, a window, the events that window consumed, and the human who approved the promotion.

## Where the analogy stops

There is no force-push and no rebase, because a fact we mirrored can change under us and the honest record of that is a new observation pointing at the old one. There is no revert either. You cannot un-send the email. That asymmetry is the reason the gate sits before the write and the correction is an append.

None of this is clever, which is the part I would defend. The model in the loop gets better a few times a year when a lab ships something, and that has stopped being the interesting variable. The record underneath gets better every week.

Start with the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/), or read how [Behaviors](/getting-started/behaviors/) are defined.

# Browser-driven verification (authenticated)

For any UI verification that needs a signed-in session (past the auth wall), use the `agent-browser` CLI with a session cookie minted from the DB. The user's regular Chrome doesn't expose a remote-debug port, so `--auto-connect` will land on the wrong tab — mint a cookie instead.

## Scope

The forged session cookie authenticates the **web admin REST mounted at `/`** (`/api/auth/*`, `/api/<orgSlug>/...`, the SPA — anything `lobu apply` and the web app talk to). It does **NOT** authenticate the **public Agent API at `/lobu`** (`/lobu/api/v1/agents/*`, `/lobu/api/v1/agents/<id>/sessions`) — that path expects a JWT bearer from the OAuth device flow (`lobu login`) or a PAT. If `/lobu/api/v1/agents` returns `401` despite a valid cookie, switch to `lobu chat` / `lobu token`.

## Pick a target

Local dev backend (with prod DB attached over Tailscale): `https://<your-tailscale-host>.ts.net:8443`. Prod: `https://app.lobu.ai`.

## Grab the secret + session token

```bash
# Local dev backend uses .env's BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
SECRET=$(grep '^BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)

# Prod uses the secret on the K8s pod
SECRET=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod \
  $(kubectl get pod -n summaries-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=lobu-app -o name | head -1 | sed 's|pod/||') \
  -- printenv BETTER_AUTH_SECRET)

# Session token from the DB (prod DB serves both targets)
DB="$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)"
TOKEN=$(psql "$DB" -tAc "SELECT token FROM session WHERE \"userId\" = '<user_id>' AND \"expiresAt\" > NOW() ORDER BY \"updatedAt\" DESC LIMIT 1")
```

## Sign the cookie

better-auth uses HMAC-SHA256, base64, then URL-encode — base64**url** does *not* validate.

```bash
SIGNED=$(SECRET="$SECRET" TOKEN="$TOKEN" node -e '
  const {createHmac}=require("node:crypto");
  const sig=createHmac("sha256",process.env.SECRET).update(process.env.TOKEN).digest("base64");
  console.log(encodeURIComponent(`${process.env.TOKEN}.${sig}`));
')
```

Cookie name is `__Secure-better-auth.session_token` whenever the baseURL is `https://` (prod and Tailscale dev qualify; only plain-http localhost uses the unprefixed `better-auth.session_token`).

## Drive the browser

```bash
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify eval "document.cookie='__Secure-better-auth.session_token=$SIGNED; path=/; secure; samesite=lax'"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/<path>"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify wait --text "<expected text>" --timeout 25000
agent-browser --session lobu-verify snapshot -i      # find @refs
agent-browser --session lobu-verify click @e13        # interact
agent-browser --session lobu-verify screenshot --full /tmp/out.png
agent-browser --session lobu-verify close
```

## Driving the paired Owletto extension (connector debugging)

The cookie-forging above and `claude-in-chrome` both drive a *separate* browser that lacks the user's real logged-in sessions — Revolut, for instance, redirects them to `sso.revolut.com/signin`. To run JS or browser actions in the **paired Owletto extension** (the Chrome that holds the user's live sessions, which is what extension-scrape connectors like Revolut/LinkedIn use), go through the connector-operations bridge instead. No deploy required.

`lobu connector run` is the wrong tool here — it only does local Playwright/CDP against a `browser_session` auth profile, so it errors `Missing --auth-profile` for device-worker connectors (Revolut has no auth profile).

All four asks landed. Refresh **http://127.0.0.1:4321/blog/self-improving-agents-are-event-sourced/**

**Links on the memory paragraph.** ChatGPT now links to the [OpenAI memory FAQ](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8590148-memory-faq), and Claude links to Anthropic's [memory tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool), which is a better citation than the consumer feature because that tool literally is a directory the model reads and writes, which is the point of the paragraph. Coding agents link to [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/).

**Numbers.** I did not round to 300k, because the real count is 229,377 and 300k would overstate it by 30% in a post whose whole argument is that the record should be honest. It now reads "the workspace Lobu runs its own company on holds roughly 230,000 events, about 27,000 of which replace an earlier observation," and later "roughly 90,000 of those 230,000 events name their run." Say the word if you want 300k anyway and I will change it.

**Docs links** added inline: `save_memory` to /getting-started/memory/, feeds to /sdks/connectors/, Behavior and reaction to /getting-started/behaviors/ and /sdks/reactions/, "which actions need a human at all is operator configuration" to /guides/tool-policy/, the MCP server to /guides/mcp-proxy/, and workspace to /getting-started/architecture/. All eight routes return 200.

**Screenshots, captured live from prod.** I used the documented `agent-browser` recipe from `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`: pulled `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` off the prod pod, minted a session cookie for your user, and drove `app.lobu.ai/lobu-team/activity`. Two figures, both real:

- **FIG_01** in the approval section: the feed filtered to `Approval: Pending`, showing a Create Issue action requested by `mcp_client_…` with its arguments rendered as an editable form (body, title with the required marker, labels, assignees, repo name, repo owner) and Confirm/Reject. That is the paragraph's claim demonstrated rather than asserted.
- **FIG_02** in the run section: one feed containing an MCP tool-invocation audit event (`agent id: lobu-builder`, `category: audit`, `event type: tool_invocation.completed`, an MCP session id, `token type: pat`, `tool name: search_sdk`), a config change event, and a rejected Create Issue action with its full JSON input. It shows the cross-agent audit trail in one frame.

Rather than reuse a landing component (blog pages load `globals.css` + `blog.css`, not `landing.css`, so those classes would not apply), I wrote `src/components/blog/ScreenshotFigure.tsx` in the same idiom as `TruthProxyDiagram`: thin border, mono `+` corner ticks, caption plate with figure number and route. Same visual language, no CSS dependency.

Credentials are wiped and the browser session is closed.

**One thing for you to look at before this ships.** Both screenshots are real prod content from our workspace. Nothing customer-facing is in them, and the GitHub issue is against our own public repo, but FIG_02 does show an MCP session UUID and a client id, and FIG_01's body text quotes an internal MCP E2E finding. Your call whether that is fine or wants a redact pass.

**Confidence**
- Screenshots are genuine and match their captions: 95. I captured, viewed, and cropped both myself.
- Link targets: 90. Eight internal routes verified 200 locally; the three external URLs come from search results this session, not from my fetching each one.
- Build/render: 85. `bun run build` green, dev server serving the new content, both webp assets resolve. Not visually reviewed at mobile width, and the new figure component has not been checked in light theme.

**Next**
1. Look at FIG_01 and FIG_02 in the page and tell me if either needs redacting or recropping.
2. Check the figure plate in light mode; I only saw the app screenshots dark, and the caption uses `--color-page-text-muted` which I have not verified in both themes.
3. Decide on 230k vs 300k.
4. Still owed: the og cover placeholder, then commit and open the landing PR (three untracked files plus the post).

Found 2026-07-30 on `legal-review.lobu.ai` (org `legal-review`, visibility `public`). Handoff doc written to `/tmp/public-workspace-rest-transport-gap.md`. UNFIXED.

**The carve-out only sees tool calls.** `canAccessPublicOrgRequest()` (`packages/server/src/workspace/multi-tenant.ts:180`) bails on `!requestedToolName` and on any non-POST/PUT/PATCH method, so a `GET /api/{org}/...` REST route can *never* be public-readable. It never reaches its handler — the middleware answers 401 (`:610`, anonymous) or 403 (`:566`, authenticated non-member).

**The bug: same data, two doors, opposite answers.** `PUBLIC_READ_ACTIONS` at `packages/server/src/auth/tool-access.ts:181` already declares `manage_agents: new Set(["list","get"])` public. Live, anonymous:
- `POST /api/legal-review/manage_agents {"action":"list"}` → **200**
- `GET  /api/legal-review/agents` → **401**

A transport gap, NOT a policy gap. The policy is written; the REST door doesn't consult it.

**Why some public pages work:** Activity uses `resolve_path` + `manage_operations.list_activity`; Connectors uses `manage_connections.list` / `manage_catalog.list_catalog` + `/api/{org}/public/*`. All tool-transport or the explicit public REST namespace → they render. The org root and the agents list use plain REST → they 401.

## Corrections from the 2026-07-30 design review (codex + prod probes) — the original handoff doc was wrong on three points

1. **`legal-review` has 0 agent rows.** Its empty sidebar is truthful data, NOT the 401. Do not use it as the witness. Use **`atlas`** (public, 2 agents incl. a system agent): there `manage_agents.list` returns both agents anonymously while `GET /api/atlas/agents` is 401. Public orgs w/ agents: atlas 2, devops/market/delivery 1 each.
2. **`/api/{org}/public/*` is NOT redundant** — do not plan to delete it. Only `behaviors` is a thin wrapper. `/public/knowledge/search` accepts MORE params than its authed sibling (`rest-api.ts:442` vs `:395`); `/public/connectors/:key` is a unique composite projection with no equivalent; `/public/organization` has no public-readable tool at all; `/public/events` applies a strict invalidation-key filter `/events` lacks. Checking one handler and generalizing to the namespace was the error.
3. **"REST has no execution-time gate" is false for 4 of 7 routes.** `connections`, `runs`, `actions/available` go through `restToolProxy` → `executeTool` → `isPublicReadable` (`tools/execute.ts:184`). Only the two agent routes and `/installed` lack it.

**The finding that reshapes the design:** `PUBLIC_READ_ACTIONS` is an *action-name* allow-list and says nothing about FIELDS. `manage_connections.list` is `SELECT c.*` (`crud.ts:270`) + a live `connect_token` subselect (`:305`). Verified anonymous on prod `market.lobu.ai`: **49 fields**, incl. `created_by`, `created_by_username`, and `connect_token` (null only because 0 tokens pending). `list_runs` returns run input/output/checkpoints; `/installed` leaks `source_uri` (can be a server-local `file://`). So "declare REST route ≡ tool action" would inherit every field — the declaration must gate the PROJECTION, not just the route.

**Design verdict:** implement projection-level capabilities with one canonical serializer per capability, or keep `(tool, action)` coupling ONLY for routes that literally proxy a fixed tool action (connections/runs/actions — which already gate at `executeTool`), and give agents + `/installed` explicit public DTOs.

**Hono seam (empirically resolved):** `c.req.routePath` returns `/api/:orgSlug/agents/*` before `next()` — useless for distinguishing list from detail. Use Hono's `routePath(c, -1)` helper, which returns `/api/:orgSlug/agents` and `/api/:orgSlug/agents/:agentId` correctly; `baseRoutePath(c, -1)` gives the mount prefix. Registry miss must deny.

**Separately, the org root is a product problem, not a policy one.** `packages/owletto/src/app/$owner.tsx:42` calls `useSystemAgentId()` unconditionally and `:110-117` renders `systemAgentError.message` verbatim. No policy change fixes it — the builder is genuinely owner-only (`set_system_agent` is in OWNER_ADMIN_ACTIONS). The root must stop requesting it for non-members. Reuse what exists: `useCurrentOrg()` → `{isMember,isPublic}`, `PublicOrgJoinBar` (already mounted in the shell), and the SSR-injected `__LOBU_PUBLIC_BOOTSTRAP__.resolvedPath.workspace`.

**Three viewer states at the org root** — only the first is fixed (by #2358):
| anonymous + private | ✅ redirect to sign-in |
| authenticated non-member + private | ❌ raw 403 |
| any non-member + public | ❌ this gap |

Before building, I checked what already exists. Three findings that change the answer:

**The homepage already has the mock app.** `HeroWindows.tsx` (1026 lines) renders the app plate with a real sidebar: Activity / Connectors / **Context**, then an Agents group with Behaviors and Guardrails. So this is not a build-from-scratch, it is a rename plus a rework of one pane.

**"Context" is stale.** The shipped app's sidebar says **Memory** (confirmed in both screenshots I took). The mock is the only place still saying Context. That rename is just correct, independent of everything else.

**The live public workspace already works, anonymously, today.** I opened `https://atlas.lobu.ai/activity` in a clean browser with no cookie: it renders the real app, real sidebar, a "You're browsing Atlas as a visitor. Sign in to join this workspace." banner, filters, and 70 real events including `tool_invocation.completed` audit rows. No build needed to link it. The catch is content: atlas's feed is deployment and config bookkeeping, its AGENTS list is empty, and there is no approval card in it. Per my notes, the public orgs are atlas (2 agents), devops, market, delivery, legal-review.

Where the mock ActivityPane actually differs from the app: it is a one-line-per-event list (`09:04 · renewalRiskMonitor wants to send a check-in to Acme Corp · Review`). The real page is a timeline of cards with a title, a key/value metadata block, and for approvals an editable form with Confirm/Reject. Matching that is a contained change to `ActivityPane` plus CSS, not a rewrite of the whole file.

One opinion before you choose: I would not swap the blog's screenshots for the mock. The post argues that the record is real and inspectable, and a hand-drawn imitation of the app is weaker evidence than a picture of the app. Mocks earn their place on the homepage, where the job is stylized and animated. The blog's job is proof.

content.text:
Checked the app, then measured what reuse would actually cost. Here is what I found and what I already fixed.

**Fixed in the homepage mock now** (`HeroWindows.tsx`, builds green):
- Sidebar row `Context` → **Memory**, including the internal view key and `ContextPane` → `MemoryPane`, so there is no half-rename left behind.
- Agent sub-rows were `Behaviors` + `Guardrails`. The app now has `Behaviors` + **Configure**, with skills/guardrails/permissions/models/settings collapsed behind it. The mock now says Configure and its pane opens with the app's workbench tab strip (Skills · Guardrails · Permissions · Models), Guardrails selected. Added one `.pill.sel` rule for the active tab.
- The app's own comment explains why Behaviors keeps its own row ("it has runtime state, so it reads as a feed, not a form"); I carried that reasoning into the mock's comment so the next person does not re-flatten it.

**On reusing the real components.** I measured it rather than guessing:

| | app (`lobu-ai/owletto`) | landing (`lobu-ai/landing`) |
|---|---|---|
| framework | React 19 | Preact 10 via Astro 6 |
| routing/data | TanStack Router + Query | none |
| UI kit | 36 shadcn components, lucide | hand-rolled `landing.css` |
| size | 72,080 LOC, 62 route files | ~4,700 LOC of landing components |

The Activity surface alone is `event-card.tsx` 2,059 lines, `events-tab/index.tsx` 1,298, filter bar 401, timeline 254, pane 236, roughly 4,250 lines, and they call `useOrgContext`, `useAgents`, `useEntityType`, `useResolvedPath`, `useSchedules`, `useAgentWatchersList` plus the router's `Link`. Importing that into landing means adding React alongside Preact, porting shadcn and the tailwind theme, stubbing six data hooks and a router context, and publishing a package across two repos that currently have no dependency between them. Then it drifts the first time someone edits the app, which is exactly the problem you are trying to solve.

**So I would invert it.** You said the mock must ideally be identical to the live screenshot. The way to guarantee that is to stop mocking and automate the capture. I confirmed the public workspaces render fully anonymously, no cookie, no auth: I opened `market.lobu.ai/activity` in a clean browser and got the real app, real sidebar (Activity / Connectors / Memory), the visitor banner, and **209,761 items** of real Reddit content with threaded replies. A capture script in the landing repo can drive that URL and write every marketing image straight from the running app. Identical by construction, refreshable on demand, and it covers all the app pages instead of just the one someone bothered to mock.

Public orgs by content, from prod:

| org | events | feeds |
|---|---|---|
| **market** | 1,385,494 | 122 |
| atlas | 212 | 0 |

**Before → after**

The old pane was five one-line rows with a `REVIEW` pill. The new one is the app's actual shape:

| filter bar | none | All / Alerts / Saved notes, chips, item count | same, compressed to 2 chips |

| approval | pill only | fields rendered from the input schema, Confirm / Reject | same, Title* and Labels with the real placeholder |
| audit row | none | key/value block: Agent id, Category, Event type, Token type | same |

The URL bar was hardcoded `/acme/context`, which my earlier rename had turned into `/acme/memory` while Activity was selected. content.text:
Retimed the mock to the product's theme. I pulled ground truth from three sources rather than guessing: the two prod screenshots already in the post, `packages/owletto/src/index.css` (the app's actual tokens), and live captures of `market.lobu.ai/connectors` and `/memory`.

What was wrong: the plate was wearing the landing page's language, not the app's. Red wash on every selected row, active segment, and input well; mono-caps on every button and badge; square corners throughout; a red lightning glyph where the app's is amber; a red-tinted "pending" row the app doesn't tint at all.

What changed:

- **One rebinding does most of it.** `.lp-hw-win.app` now sets `--lp-wash: var(--lp-dim)` (the app's `--accent` / `#211E1A`), so all eight red-wash sites inside the plate — activity, behaviors, guardrails, chat, the segmented control, the input wells — go neutral at once. Red is now spent only where the app spends it: the primary button, the required-field asterisk, the send button.
- **Sidebar** matches: rows carry their own padding and a filled block for the selected one, nav icons stay muted (they were red), and there's now the workspace switcher the app pins to the top — `A Acme ⌄` with search and collapse.
- **Radius.** New `--lp-r: 6px`, scoped to the plate only. Chips, inputs, buttons, connector cards, graph nodes, the composer and the menu are rounded; the window frame and the rest of the page stay flat.
- **Badges and buttons** are sentence-case sans with glyphs (`✓ Confirm` / `✕ Reject`, `Data`, `Actions`, `Needs setup`, `Behavior run`, `2 tool calls`, `Send`) instead of mono-caps boxes. The guardrail switch is now a pill that fills with the accent, as shadcn draws it.
- **Bolt is amber** (`#c8931f`), sampled off the real screenshot — it was red.
- **Connectors** got the app's bordered list card and neutral "Needs setup" badge; the real page's is gray, not red.
- **Memory canvas** lost the dot grid and the boxed zoom stepper — `market.lobu.ai/memory` renders on a plain surface with a borderless control.
- Two small correctness fixes on the way: Configure's address bar said `/skills` while the Guardrails tab was selected, and the Slack/Claude/API transcripts all said `/acme/activity`. They now use the real routes (`/acme/agents/scout/guardrails`, `/acme/agents/scout/chat/c/{id}`).

Verified all six panes in dark and connectors + activity in light. `bun run build` green.

**Confidence: 85** — every pane captured and compared against a real screenshot at plate size, but three panes (Skills/Permissions/Models under Configure, Claude and API transcripts) I only reasoned about through shared CSS rather than eyeballing, and I have no live capture of the real Behaviors or agent-chat page since the public workspaces have no agents.

**Next**
1. Decide the three remaining `lp-hw-foot` footers — Activity's "append-only · 1 awaiting approval", Behaviors', Configure's. The real app has no such footer, and it's the same species as the connectors one you cut.
2. The sidebar RECENT group has no app equivalent either; it's currently the only way into the Slack/Claude/API plates.
3. `activity-approval.webp` / `activity-audit.webp` in the blog post are dark-mode captures — they'll sit inside a light blog page unless we recapture or accept the contrast.
4. og cover is still the `[ NO PLATE ]` placeholder, and the landing PR is unopened.

CELL = 20
grid = Image.new('RGBA', (7, 7), (0, 0, 0, 0))
for x, y, w, h in rects:
    for gx in range(x // CELL, (x + w) // CELL):

    off = (s - 7 * k) // 2

    frames.append(f)

         re.findall(r'<rect x="(\d+)" y="(\d+)" width="(\d+)" height="(\d+)"', src)]
CELL = 20
grid = Image.new('RGBA', (7, 7), (0, 0, 0, 0))
for x, y, w, h in rects:
    for gx in range(x // CELL, (x + w) // CELL):
        for gy in range(y // CELL, (y + h) // CELL):
            grid.putpixel((gx, gy), (245, 51, 58, 255))

sizes = [16, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256]
frames = []
for s in sizes:
    # Largest whole-pixel cell that still leaves an even margin, so the mark is
    # both crisp and centred. Anything else lands a cell on a half pixel.
    k = max(k for k in range(1, s // 7 + 1) if (s - 7 * k) % 2 == 0)
    art = grid.resize((7 * k, 7 * k), Image.NEAREST)
    f = Image.new('RGBA', (s, s), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    off = (s - 7 * k) // 2
    f.paste(art, (off, off))
    frames.append(f)
    print(f'{s:>3} cell={k}px margin={off}px')

frames[-1].save('public/favicon.ico', format='ICO',

It's not broken as a file — it returns 200 and is a valid 6-size ICO. It's the **wrong logo**. `public/favicon.ico` still holds the old red *fish* mark on a white square, from commit `614034d` ("favicon is the red fish mark"). The brand moved to the pixel claw and the ico never followed:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| mark | fish | claw (matches `lobu-mark.svg`) |
| background | opaque white | transparent |
| size | 15,440 B | 2,376 B |
| frames | 16/32/48/64/128/256 | same |

That's also why it looked fine to you in some places and wrong in others: `BaseLayout.astro:62` serves `/lobu-mark.svg` as the primary `rel="icon"`, and Chrome/Firefox prefer the SVG. Everything that ignores it and just fetches `/favicon.ico` — Google's result favicons, Safari, most crawlers and link unfurlers — got the fish.

Regenerated it from `lobu-mark.svg` directly. The mark is a 7×7 pixel grid, so I rebuilt the grid from the SVG's rects and scaled with nearest-neighbour, picking per size the largest whole-pixel cell that still leaves an even margin — otherwise a cell lands on a half pixel and the pixel art goes soft. Read back all six frames: each contains exactly two colours, `#F5333A` and full transparency, so nothing got interpolated.

```
 16 cell=2px  margin=1px      16 colours=2 crisp=True
 32 cell=4px  margin=2px      32 colours=2 crisp=True
 48 cell=6px  margin=3px      48 colours=2 crisp=True
 64 cell=8px  margin=4px      64 colours=2 crisp=True
128 cell=18px margin=1px     128 colours=2 crisp=True
256 cell=36px margin=2px     256 colours=2 crisp=True
```

`git status --short` → ` M public/favicon.ico`, the only changed file. It's binary, so the render above is the diff.

One adjacent thing I did **not** change: `BaseLayout.astro:64` sets `apple-touch-icon` to `/lobu-mark.png`, which is 34% opaque. iOS composites transparent touch icons onto black, so a home-screen bookmark gets a red claw on black rather than on the brand background. That's a different defect from this one, so it's your call.

**Confidence: 95** — regenerated from the canonical SVG and verified every frame's pixel content by reading the written file back; the 5% is that I haven't seen it served from a deploy yet.

**Next**
1. Deploy and re-check `curl https://lobu.ai/favicon.ico | file -` — prod cache is `max-age=14400, must-revalidate`, so ~4h for the stale one to clear on already-visited clients.
2. Decide on the `apple-touch-icon` transparency (a 512 PNG with `#0F0E0C` or white behind the claw).
3. Google Search Console favicon re-crawl if you want the search result icon updated sooner than its own schedule.
4. Still open from before: the three `lp-hw-foot` pane footers, the sidebar RECENT group, the `[ NO PLATE ]` og cover, and the unopened landing PR — which now has a favicon fix riding in it.

---
title: "The Modern Data Stack for Agents"
description: "Connectors are CDC, entities are the modelled tables, Behaviors are dbt models on a schedule. The analogy is worth taking seriously, and worth knowing where it breaks: the loop closes, the cache stays demoted, the scope travels with the read, and the transform is unsafe to repeat."
date: 2026-07-29
author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
tags: [architecture, agents, memory, analytics]
cover: /design/prim-agent-warehouse.webp
draft: false
---

Every team building agent memory ends up rebuilding the modern data stack, usually without noticing. You start with "the agent should remember things," you add a sync from Slack, then one from your CRM, then you need the same person from both to be one person, then someone asks why the agent said 40 and the dashboard says 38. That is not a novel AI problem. That is ingestion, modelling, and reconciliation, and data engineering spent fifteen years on it.

So it is worth taking the analogy seriously, because most of it transfers. Connectors are change data capture. The append-only log is your raw landing zone. Entities are the modelled tables. Behaviors are dbt models on a schedule. The app is the BI layer on top. If you have built a warehouse you already know how most of an agent memory layer should be shaped, and you should reuse that instinct rather than inventing vocabulary.

![The classic pipeline: OLTP systems, change capture, warehouse tables, analysts, executives, and then nothing. The conveyor ends in mid-air and the out-tray is empty](/blog/warehouse-pipeline.webp)

Then it breaks, in four specific places. The breakages are what the rest of this is about.

## A warehouse is terminal. This one writes back.

Look at the pipeline above and follow it to the end. An analyst reads the dashboard, writes a brief, and an executive decides something. Whatever happens next leaves the system. The decision might land in Slack, or a board deck, or nowhere. The warehouse has no idea it happened, and next quarter's model has no way to learn that the March number was thrown out for a reason.

Warehouses do push data back out, and reverse ETL is a mature category, so the store is not literally a dead end. You could model decisions as a table and sync them, and some teams do. What makes it rare is that nothing in the pipeline captures the decision in the first place: it happens in a meeting, or a Slack thread, and reaches the warehouse only if a human remembers to write it down. Capture is the hard part, and a system whose consumers are agents has to solve it at the point of decision rather than hoping for a later backfill.

![The same shape for agents: the log, the run, shaped data, and the interfaces that write back](/blog/agent-warehouse.webp)

So the loop closes. When an agent wants to do something consequential, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. The human's decision is not an update to that event; it appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with who decided. The action's outcome supersedes again later, carrying the output or the error. The approval, the rejection, the arguments a reviewer edited before letting it through: all of it is in the same store the agent reads from tomorrow.

That is the difference between a system that reports and a system that improves. I wrote about the store underneath that loop in [The Context Layer Is an Event Store](/blog/the-context-layer-is-an-event-store/).

I rewrote its alt text, which had gone factually wrong. The old one ended "the conveyor ends in mid-air and the out-tray is empty" — that described the old drawing literally, and the new one has a labelled return band along the bottom instead.

One thing for you to decide, because it's your argument and not mine to rewrite. Directly under the figure the post says:

The new image contradicts that on its face — its bottom band reads that manual actions "re-enter source systems and become new operational events." content.text:
No, we don't. Both figures are the Activity page — one under "The human review step is a merge," one under "Every run writes to the same log." The Behaviors section is the longest figure-free stretch in the post, which is a shame, because it's the section whose claim is the most visual:

> A Behavior is a trigger, a prompt, and optional named SQL sources over the events log... It appends events... Or it changes entities.

The mock already renders exactly that. `BehaviorsPane` in `HeroWindows.tsx:507` shows each behavior expanding into **Triggers** (connector events plus a clock), the goal prompt, and **Writes** split into entity changes vs events back to the log. That's the paragraph as a picture.

What's missing is only the extraction: `ActivityPane` takes a config, `BehaviorsPane` still has its data hardcoded at `HeroWindows.tsx:457`. Same treatment — move it to `app-plate/BehaviorsPane.tsx`, give it a `BehaviorsConfig` — and it drops into the post as FIG_02, renumbering the other two.

The part I don't want to guess at is the content. The three behaviors in the hero are the Acme sales fiction (renewal risk, churn signals, Monday brief), and both existing figures in this post are Lobu's own workspace — Lobu Team, the `lobu` repo, a real `mcp_client_` id. Dropping Acme in between would break that, and inventing plausible-looking Lobu behaviors would put fabricated product facts in a published post.

Two ways to go:

1. I query the Lobu Team workspace for its actual behaviors and build the figure from those, matching how the other two figures are grounded.
2. You tell me the three you want depicted and I'll write them.

Either way the extraction is the same work and I can have it done in one pass. Which?

22	Look at the pipeline above and follow it to the end. An analyst reads the dashboard, writes a brief, and an executive decides something. Whatever happens next leaves the system. The decision might land in Slack, or a board deck, or nowhere. The warehouse has no idea it happened, and next quarter's model has no way to learn that the March number was thrown out for a reason.
23	
24	Warehouses do push data back out, and reverse ETL is a mature category, so the store is not literally a dead end. You could model decisions as a table and sync them, and some teams do. What makes it rare is that nothing in the pipeline captures the decision in the first place: it happens in a meeting, or a Slack thread, and reaches the warehouse only if a human remembers to write it down. Capture is the hard part, and a system whose consumers are agents has to solve it at the point of decision rather than hoping for a later backfill.
25	
26	![The same six stages rebuilt for agents: sources, an ingestion gateway that collects, normalizes and validates, the append-only event log, the agents that subscribe and run and request approval, live entities kept in the loop, and the interfaces a human reviews them through. Along the bottom, every output, approval and human interaction becomes a new event, closing the loop the traditional stack leaves open](/blog/agent-warehouse.webp)
27	
28	So the loop closes. When an agent wants to do something consequential, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. The human's decision is not an update to that event; it appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with who decided. The action's outcome supersedes again later, carrying the output or the error. The approval, the rejection, the arguments a reviewer edited before letting it through: all of it is in the same store the agent reads from tomorrow.
29	
30	That is the difference between a system that reports and a system that improves. I wrote about the store underneath that loop in [The Context Layer Is an Event Store](/blog/the-context-layer-is-an-event-store/).
31

content.text: Both done and pushed. New preview is building; I'll hand over the URL when it lands. **Cover swap.** `the-modern-data-stack-for-agents` now uses `/blog/agent-warehouse.webp` as its cover, replacing `/design/prim-agent-warehouse.webp`. I also removed the in-body copy — the layout renders the cover as FIG_01 at prose width, so keeping both put the identical image on the page twice. Net effect: that post opens with the agent-stack diagram and keeps the traditional pipeline in the body where the argument needs it. **Behaviors figure.** Extracted `BehaviorsPane` next to `ActivityPane`, config-driven, and dropped it into the post right after "A Behavior is a mutation against your data model." GitHub-flavoured as you asked, three of them: - **Triage what lands in the tracker** — `issue.opened`, `issue.labeled`, hourly → sets the component and severity on the Issue entity, appends `triage.linked`. Asks before closing a duplicate. - **Keep the docs honest** — Notion `page.updated`, Drive `doc.revised`, `pull_request.merged` → supersedes the facts an edited spec changed, appends `contradiction.flagged`. That's the people-changing-documents one, and it lands on the post's own supersede vocabulary. - **Say what shipped** — Mondays 9:00 → `message.sent`. No approval needed, so the pane shows all three trigger kinds and both write shapes. Two things I hit on the way: The prompt rendered as an **empty band** at first. A JSX fragment written inside a prop object in MDX doesn't survive the Astro→Preact boundary — the children pass fine, but a vnode nested in a plain object renders as nothing. `goal` is now a string with `*emphasis*` markers, which also makes the config properly serializable. Both call sites converted; verified the bolds survive in the hero (`blocker reopens`, `customer`, `#sales`, `ask before`) and in the figure (`component`, `Ask before`). The post was showing **two FIG_01s** — the layout hardcodes `FIG_01` for the cover plate. Body figures now run FIG_02 (Behaviors), FIG_03 (approval form), FIG_04 (mixed feed). I also dropped `role="img"` from `AppFigure` in favour of a visually-hidden description. The Behaviors rows expand, and `role="img"` would have hidden working controls from a screen reader while leaving them keyboard-focusable. **Your mobile fix was already on the branch** — `c439e9a`, collapsing the figure sidebar under 640px. I rebased onto it rather than force-pushing over it, so it's intact. Verified: build green (74 pages), `tsc --noEmit` clean, hero Behaviors pane clicked through on a fresh dev server, figure screenshotted. Worth noting the dev server had gone stale and was serving old content for a while — the frontmatter change and the goal fix both only showed after a restart, so treat anything you looked at on 4321 in the last while with suspicion. **Confidence: 90** — every claim above checked in a browser or in built HTML rather than inferred. The 8–10% is light mode, which I still haven't looked at on any of the figures. **Next** 1. Light-mode pass — the only gap left from my original list now that mobile is handled. 2. The cover `` has `alt=""` in the layout, which was fine for decorative art but that cover is now a text-dense infographic. A `coverAlt` frontmatter field is ~3 additive lines if you want it. 3. this is what eanother agent told about the warehouse post, the implications? Worked for 1m 53s

As currently drawn, it risks looking like medallion architecture. Raw events go in, a machine transforms them, structured entities come out, and dashboards appear. That visual alone is not enough to communicate what is new.

But the Lobu architecture is not merely a data warehouse or medallion pipeline.

The distinction
Medallion architecture    Lobu’s agent architecture
Bronze → silver → gold    Events → triggered behaviors → live entity state
Improves data quality through stages    Runs agents when subscribed events occur
Primarily produces tables for querying    Produces entity changes, actions, approvals, and new events
Mostly read-oriented    Read-write and operational
Usually ends at BI or downstream apps    Interfaces and conversations are part of the runtime
Data flows predominantly forward    Every interaction can append another event
Transformation jobs    Stateful agent executions with tools and permissions

Parts of Lobu can resemble medallion architecture:

The append-only event log resembles a raw or bronze layer.
Resolved entities resemble curated silver or gold models.
Dashboards resemble traditional consumption surfaces.

But that is only the data plane. The differentiator is the operational loop:

A behavior subscribes to events, runs an agent, reads existing entities and history, uses tools, emits entity changes or new events, and may involve a human through an approval, form, brief, activity page, or conversation.

That is much closer to a combination of:

event sourcing
materialized views
stream processing
workflow orchestration
agent runtime
human-in-the-loop applications
Is “data warehouse for agents” valid?

It is a useful hook, but not the complete category.

A data warehouse gave analysts:

durable shared history
structured models
consistent definitions
a place to query company data

Agents need all of that, but also:

subscriptions and triggers
continuously maintained entities
tools and actions
permissions
approvals
write-back
interfaces
auditable agent runs

So the sharper statement is:

Agents need what a data warehouse gave analysts—but operational, event-driven, and writable.

Or:

A data warehouse for agents is necessary, but not sufficient.

Better category

I would position it as:

The Operational Data Stack for Agents

Subtitle:

Event logs, live entities, triggered behaviors, human interfaces, and write-back for long-running agents.

That is more accurate than “The Modern Data Stack, Rebuilt for Agents.” The latter makes readers expect ETL, lakehouses, dbt, and BI. Your thesis is that agents extend the data stack into the operational/application layer.

Another strong blog title is:

Agents Need More Than a Data Warehouse

Why production agents require events, live entities, behaviors, approvals, and write-back.

That title lets you deliberately introduce the warehouse analogy, then show where it breaks.

The corrected architecture

The public-facing flow should be:

Sources → Ingestion → Event Log → Behaviors → Live Entity State → Interfaces

But behavior has two outputs, not one:

                           ┌──→ Entity changes ──→ Live entity state
Event log → Behavior run ──┤
                           └──→ New events ──────→ Event log

Then interfaces also write back:

Live entity state → Activity / Approvals / Briefs / Forms / Agent
                                      │
                                      └──→ Human actions → New events

This matters because a behavior is not a generic transformation stage. It is:

A subscription that runs an agent in response to matching events.

For example:

contract_uploaded
        ↓
Contract-review behavior runs
        ↓
Reads contract, customer, deal, policies and prior decisions
        ↓
Updates Contract entity
Creates Risk entity
Emits approval_requested event
        ↓
Lawyer reviews approval
        ↓
approval_accepted event
        ↓
Another behavior drafts the redline and updates the CRM

That cannot be adequately described as bronze → silver → gold.

How the cover should change

The current image should avoid “shaped data”, because that sounds like a warehouse transformation layer.

Use these labels:

SOURCES
INGESTION
EVENT LOG
TRIGGERED BEHAVIORS
LIVE ENTITIES
INTERFACES

The behavior machine should visibly have two exits:

ENTITY CHANGES going toward the entity cabinet
NEW EVENTS / ACTIONS returning to the log

The interfaces should include:

activity
approvals
briefs
forms
freeform agent conversation

And every interface should have an arrow returning to the event log.

Also show a traditional data warehouse as one possible source, alongside CRM, email, documents, and databases. That communicates that Lobu does not replace the warehouse; it operationalizes data from it and other systems.

The clearest central message for the graphic is:

Events trigger agents. Agents update entities and create new events. People interact through interfaces, creating the next events.

That is the concept. The warehouse analogy helps introduce it, but the operational agent loop is the actual product.
