On the critique — I checked it against the image that's actually on the branch, and **most of it was written against the previous diagram, not the current one.**

The tell is `"The current image should avoid 'shaped data'"`. `SHAPED DATA` was a label on the *old* `agent-warehouse.webp`, the one we replaced an hour ago. The new one doesn't contain that phrase. And its recommended labels — SOURCES, INGESTION, EVENT LOG, TRIGGERED BEHAVIORS, LIVE ENTITIES, INTERFACES — match the new cover five-for-six verbatim:

```
① SOURCES / OLTP   ② INGESTION   ③ EVENT LOG   ④ AGENTS   ⑤ LIVE ENTITIES   ⑥ INTERFACES
```

Stage ④ is the only difference, and inside that box it already reads BEHAVIOR ENGINE / SUBSCRIBE (on events) / RUN (agent, tools) / REQUEST APPROVAL (if needed). The bottom band already says "NEW EVENTS — agent outputs, approvals, and human interactions create new events," captioned "A CONTINUOUS OPERATIONAL LOOP." The two-exits requirement and the interfaces-write-back requirement are both drawn.

The prose advice has the same problem. "That title lets you deliberately introduce the warehouse analogy, then show where it breaks" is the post's existing structure — it says "Then it breaks, in four specific places. The breakages are what the rest of this is about," and the first breakage is literally "A warehouse is terminal. This one writes back."

So three things actually survive:

**The warehouse-as-a-source point is the real one.** The sources column is CRM, EMAIL, DOCUMENTS, DATABASES, PRODUCT/APP — no warehouse. Drawing one there changes the positioning claim from "we're the warehouse for agents" to "we operationalize your warehouse," which is a different and more defensible thing to say to anyone who already has Snowflake. That's a regeneration, not an edit.

**The title is a genuine open question, and it's cheap.** One inbound link (the event-sourcing post), and the post is already live on prod at that slug, so a slug change needs a line in `public/_redirects` — you have 28 already, so the machinery exists. Retitling without changing the slug costs nothing at all.

**One implication neither of us had before: we raised the stakes on the diagram today.** By making it the cover, it became the og image. It's now what unfurls on every share of that post — seen by people who don't read the four breakages. The medallion misread was previously a risk for someone skimming mid-article; now it's the first and often only thing an X or LinkedIn reader sees. That's an argument for the warehouse-as-source fix specifically, more than for the title.

Where I'd push back on the other agent: "necessary but not sufficient" is exactly what the post argues, and a title that states its own qualification ("Agents Need More Than a Data Warehouse") gives away the turn. "The Modern Data Stack for Agents" is a hook the body immediately complicates, which is a legitimate structure, not a mistake. If you do retitle, I'd retitle for reach, not for accuracy.

Nothing changed on the branch — this is analysis only.

# First 5 Paragraphs

"[SIMD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_instruction,_multiple_data) has a reputation for being complex. I've met many very good software engineers who dismiss it as something too complex to learn or a niche optimization meant for only the highest-performance software, not useful in everyday programming.

I think that's wrong. SIMD can be simple to understand, and common "process N values at a time" SIMD code to speed up a naive for loop almost always follows the same general shape. Once you learn the basics, writing SIMD is just about as easy as a for loop. And when it's not, it's usually a good sign to skip it for now.

Every developer should know at least that much SIMD.

This post uses Zig for examples but is a general piece that applies to any programming language. Support for SIMD instructions varies by programming language and I hope that more programming languages expose these generic concepts in the future!

I hate that I have to do this for every post now, but I also want to note this was completely hand-written with no AI assistance."

---

# Teaching Strategy for Technical Concepts

Hashimoto introduces unfamiliar material through progressive exposure:

**Definitions precede application**: He defines SIMD before showing its code implementation, establishing foundational understanding before complexity.

**Concrete reformulation**: Rather than abstract explanation, he shows how familiar loops like "for (byte in bytes)" become "for (8 byte chunk in bytes)"—replacing technical jargon with recognizable patterns.

**Accessibility through reassurance**: He frames SIMD as learnable, stating "writing SIMD is just about as easy as a for loop," reducing perceived intimidation.

**Structured decomposition**: Complex code gets broken into five distinct, labeled steps, allowing readers to absorb concepts sequentially rather than facing overwhelming detail simultaneously.

**Layered sentence variety**: Short, punchy sentences ("That's the basics.") alternate with longer explanatory passages, maintaining engagement while preventing cognitive overload.

content.text:
I read a couple of his posts to ground this rather than working from impression. The pattern that matters:

He names a belief and disagrees with it in the first line — *"SIMD has a reputation for being complex... I think that's wrong."* He drops a one-sentence paragraph when something matters — *"Every developer should know at least that much SIMD."* He defines before he uses. And instead of naming a concept, he shows the familiar thing it replaces: `for (byte in bytes)` becomes `for (8 byte chunk in bytes)`.

Here's what that looks like against your densest paragraph, from the event-sourcing post:

**Now**
> The chain is enforced, not conventional. A partial unique index means at most one event can supersede a given target, so the loser of a concurrent-supersede race gets a `23505` and a real error instead of a fork. Current state is a view over that: an event is current if nothing supersedes it.

**In that voice**
> None of this relies on the agent behaving. The database only lets one event replace a given fact. If two agents try to replace the same fact at the same moment, the second one gets an error instead of quietly creating a second version of the truth.
>
> So "what is true right now" isn't a field anyone maintains. A fact is current if nothing has replaced it. That's the whole rule.

Same claims, no `23505`, no "partial unique index," and the point arrives before the mechanism instead of after it.

One thing I'd push back on before doing this everywhere. The two posts are jargon-heavy for different reasons. In the event-sourcing post it's incidental — `semantic_type`, `supersedes_event_id`, advisory locks, error codes — and cutting it costs nothing. In the data-stack post the jargon *is* the argument: "connectors are CDC, Behaviors are dbt models on a schedule" only lands for someone who knows what dbt is, and that reader is the one the post is written for. De-jargoning that one would blunt its thesis. I'd translate the surrounding prose there but keep the analogy terms.

Also worth knowing: both are already published and live, and the data-stack post just changed slug an hour ago.

3	description: "Connectors are CDC, entities are the modelled tables, Behaviors are dbt models on a schedule. The analogy is worth taking seriously, and worth knowing where it breaks: the loop closes, the cache stays demoted, the scope travels with the read, and the transform is unsafe to repeat."
4	date: 2026-07-29
5	author: Burak Emre Kabakcı

10	---
11	
12	Every team building agent memory ends up rebuilding the modern data stack, usually without noticing. You start with "the agent should remember things," you add a sync from Slack, then one from your CRM, then you need the same person from both to be one person, then someone asks why the agent said 40 and the dashboard says 38. That is not a novel AI problem. That is ingestion, modelling, and reconciliation, and data engineering spent fifteen years on it.
13	
14	So it is worth taking the analogy seriously, because most of it transfers. Connectors are change data capture. The append-only log is your raw landing zone. Entities are the modelled tables. Behaviors are dbt models on a schedule. The app is the BI layer on top. If you have built a warehouse you already know how most of an agent memory layer should be shaped, and you should reuse that instinct rather than inventing vocabulary.
15	
16	![The classic pipeline in six numbered stages: OLTP sources, CDC and ETL, the data warehouse of fact tables, dimensions and aggregates, analysts, executives, and end users. Along the bottom, the manual actions those people take re-enter the source systems as new operational events, never as a record of the decision itself](/blog/warehouse-pipeline.webp)
17	
18	Then it breaks, in four specific places. The breakages are what the rest of this is about.
19	
20	## A warehouse is terminal. This one writes back.
21	
22	Look at the pipeline above and follow it to the end. An analyst reads the dashboard, writes a brief, and an executive decides something. Whatever happens next leaves the system. The decision might land in Slack, or a board deck, or nowhere. The warehouse has no idea it happened, and next quarter's model has no way to learn that the March number was thrown out for a reason.
23	
24	Warehouses do push data back out, and reverse ETL is a mature category, so the store is not literally a dead end. You could model decisions as a table and sync them, and some teams do. What makes it rare is that nothing in the pipeline captures the decision in the first place: it happens in a meeting, or a Slack thread, and reaches the warehouse only if a human remembers to write it down. Capture is the hard part, and a system whose consumers are agents has to solve it at the point of decision rather than hoping for a later backfill.
25	
26	So the loop closes. When an agent wants to do something consequential, one transaction writes a pending run and a pending approval event. The human's decision is not an update to that event; it appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with who decided. The action's outcome supersedes again later, carrying the output or the error. The approval, the rejection, the arguments a reviewer edited before letting it through: all of it is in the same store the agent reads from tomorrow.
27	
28	That is the difference between a system that reports and a system that improves. I wrote about the store underneath that loop in [The Context Layer Is an Event Store](/blog/the-context-layer-is-an-event-store/).
29	
30	## Derived state, not staged tiers
31	
32	The instinct from warehouse-land is medallion: bronze for raw, silver for cleaned, gold for business-level aggregates. Three tiers, each a physical table you maintain, each authoritative for its own layer.
33	
34	We materialize too, so this is not projection versus materialization. Those are not alternatives, and anyone who has built a read model knows it. The difference is what the materialized table is allowed to claim, and the clearest way to say it is with one we deleted.
35	
36	For a day in June there was a trigger-maintained table holding the latest value of every entity field. The comment on it demoted the table in its own description, calling itself a rebuildable cache and naming the events log as the source of truth. Then we dropped it, because no read path ever consumed it and the producer feeding it was pure overhead on the hot write path. That took one migration. The events it had emitted stayed in the log, because the log is never rewritten, and they are still there if we ever want the projection back.
37	
38	That is what "not a tier" buys you. A silver table is authoritative for its layer, so deleting it is a data-loss event and rebuilding it is a project. A cache is a guess you are allowed to be wrong about. The shape is closer to what Jay Kreps called [kappa architecture](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/questioning-the-lambda-architecture/) than to a medallion stack: one immutable log, everything downstream derivable from it, and nothing downstream load-bearing.
39	
40	The distinction sounds academic until you have to correct something. When silver is authoritative, fixing a bad row means a backfill and a reconciliation, and "what did gold say last Tuesday" often has no answer. Here the correction is an append pointing at what it replaced, anything derived recomputes from the log, and the old value is still on disk. You are paying storage for the ability to answer questions about your own past, which is a trade worth making when the thing being explained is an agent's mistake.
41	
42	## Warehouses do not ask who is asking. This one has to.
43	
44	This is the difference that surprised me most, and the one I would push hardest on if you are building this.
45	
46	Warehouses can do this and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Snowflake row access policies and dynamic masking are enforced by the engine, in the query path, not by whichever dashboard someone opened. The mechanism is there and it is good.
47	
48	What differs is the shape of the consumer. Warehouse policies key off a session identity: the role executing the query. That works when each human logs in as themselves. An agent breaks the assumption, because one process serves everybody, and the identity that matters is the person the agent is answering for, not the credential it connected with. Get that wrong once and a coworker's Gmail ends up in an answer, with no dashboard boundary to catch it.
49	
50	So every read carries an explicit scope rather than inheriting one from the connection. Org scoping, per-connection visibility, and per-resource membership all become part of the SQL that runs. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private by a database trigger. When a membership sync goes stale the gate fails closed, so a stalled sync hides data instead of leaking it.
51	
52	None of this is beyond a warehouse. You can bind a request-scoped identity and let engine-level policies do the work, and that is the right way to build it. The difference is that a warehouse lets you defer it, because a missing policy usually surfaces as a dashboard nobody can open. An agent turns the same gap into a plausible sentence containing somebody else's data, so the scope has to be mandatory on every read rather than something you add when the compliance review lands.
53	
54	## The transform is not idempotent
55	
56	The closest thing we have to a dbt model is a Behavior: a declared unit of work that runs on a cadence, reads the log, and writes derived events back. Underneath, a tick enqueues a row on a job queue, and that row is the unit of execution, moving through pending, claimed, and running with heartbeat-based reaping when a worker dies. If you have configured a Snowflake Task or an Airflow DAG, you already know this shape.
57	
58	Then it stops being familiar. Re-running a dbt model is usually cheap and usually safe. Not always: incremental models and snapshots carry state, sources move underneath you, and a full refresh on a large table costs real money. But the failure mode is a wrong table or a bigger bill, which is why the ecosystem can treat re-running as the default recovery strategy. When something looks wrong, you run it again.
59	
60	A Behavior calls a model and can take actions in systems we do not own. It sends the email. There is no `--full-refresh` that unsends it, and no amount of compute buys the message back. That single property is why the machinery around it looks stricter than a warehouse's: why a run is claimed rather than merely scheduled, why the claim query only ever selects approved work, and why an approval is a durable event rather than a flag someone flips in a UI. The orchestration is heavier because the failure mode is not a stale table.
61	
62	## What the warehouse still does better
63	
64	If your question is analytical, a warehouse wins and it is not close. Columnar storage and decades of query optimization beat a Postgres event log for scanning a billion rows to get one aggregate, and the dbt ecosystem around it is better than anything we would build. We do not compete there. Metrics that need the warehouse read the warehouse, live, over a connector, and the answer is composed rather than copied.
65	
66	So the claim is narrower than replacing anything. Agent memory should borrow warehouse practice for ingestion, modelling, and provenance, because that work is done and it is good. What it cannot borrow is the shape: the loop has to close, derived state has to stay demoted to a cache, the scope has to travel with the read, and the transform has to be treated as unsafe to repeat. None of those four come from AI being special. They come from a consumer that acts on what it finds, in systems nobody here owns.
67	
68	The truth stays in the systems that own it. What this store keeps is what was observed, who may see it, and what every agent did about it.
69	
70	Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.
71

---
title: "The Operational Data Stack for Agents"
description: "Connectors are CDC, entities are the modelled tables, Behaviors are dbt models on a schedule. Most of the analogy transfers. It breaks in four places: the loop has to close, derived state is only ever a cache, every read carries who it is for, and you cannot re-run a transform that sends email."
date: 2026-07-29
author: Burak Emre Kabakcı
authorUrl: https://x.com/bu7emba
tags: [architecture, agents, memory, analytics]
cover: /blog/agent-warehouse.webp
draft: false
---

Every team building agent memory ends up rebuilding the modern data stack. Most don't notice until they are most of the way through.

It starts with "the agent should remember things." You add a sync from Slack. Then one from your CRM. Then you need the same person from both sources to be one person. Then someone asks why the agent said 40 when the dashboard says 38.

None of that is an AI problem. It is ingestion, modelling, and reconciliation, and data engineering spent fifteen years working it out.

So take the analogy seriously, because most of it transfers. Connectors are change data capture. The append-only log is your raw landing zone. Entities are the modelled tables. Behaviors are dbt models on a schedule. The app is the BI layer on top. If you have built a warehouse, you already know most of the shape an agent memory layer should have, and you should reuse that instinct instead of inventing new vocabulary.

![The classic pipeline in six numbered stages: OLTP sources, CDC and ETL, the data warehouse of fact tables, dimensions and aggregates, analysts, executives, and end users. Along the bottom, the manual actions those people take re-enter the source systems as new operational events, never as a record of the decision itself](/blog/warehouse-pipeline.webp)

It breaks in four places. Those four are the rest of this post.

## Writing the decision back

Follow the pipeline above to the end. An analyst reads a dashboard, writes a brief, an executive decides something.

Then the decision leaves. Some of what people do next comes back as raw activity, a new row or a new ticket, but the decision itself never does. It lands in Slack, or a board deck, or nowhere. The warehouse never learns it happened, so next quarter's model has no way to know the March number was thrown out for a reason.

Warehouses do push data back out. Reverse ETL is a mature category, you could model decisions as a table and sync them, and some teams do. What makes it rare is that nothing upstream captures the decision in the first place. It happens in a meeting or a Slack thread and reaches the warehouse only if somebody remembers to write it down.

Capture is the hard part. A store whose readers are agents has to catch the decision where it is made, not backfill it afterwards.

So we close the loop. When an agent wants to do something consequential, one transaction writes two things: a pending run, and an event saying a human needs to approve it.

The human's answer does not update that event. It appends a new one pointing at it, stamped with who decided. Later the outcome appends again, carrying whatever came back. The approval, the rejection, the arguments a reviewer edited before letting it through: all of it lands in the same store the agent reads from tomorrow.

I wrote about the store underneath that loop in [The Context Layer Is an Event Store](/blog/the-context-layer-is-an-event-store/).

## Everything downstream is only a cache

The instinct from warehouse-land is medallion: bronze for raw, silver for cleaned, gold for business-level aggregates. Three tiers, each a physical table you maintain, each authoritative for its own layer.

We materialize too, so this is not projection versus materialization. Anyone who has built a read model knows those are not alternatives. The difference is what the materialized table is allowed to claim.

The clearest way to explain it is with one we deleted.

For a day in June we had a trigger-maintained table holding the latest value of every entity field. Its own comment demoted it, calling itself a rebuildable cache and naming the events log as the source of truth. Then we dropped it, because no read path consumed it and the producer feeding it was pure overhead on the hot write path. That took one migration. The events it had emitted stayed in the log, because we never rewrite the log, and they are still there if we want the projection back.

Try that with a silver table. It is authoritative for its layer, so deleting it loses data and rebuilding it is a project. Ours was a cache, and a cache is allowed to be wrong. The shape is closer to what Jay Kreps called [kappa architecture](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/questioning-the-lambda-architecture/) than to a medallion stack: one immutable log, everything downstream derived from it, nothing downstream load-bearing.

This sounds academic until you have to correct something. When silver is authoritative, fixing a bad row means a backfill and a reconciliation, and "what did gold say last Tuesday" often has no answer at all. Here a correction is an append pointing at what it replaced, anything derived recomputes from the log, and the old value is still on disk. You pay storage for the ability to answer questions about your own past. That is a good trade when the thing you are explaining is an agent's mistake.

## Every read has to carry who it is for

This is the difference that surprised me most, and the one I would push hardest on if you are building this.

Warehouses can do it, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Snowflake row access policies and dynamic masking run in the query path, enforced by the engine rather than by whichever dashboard someone happened to open. The mechanism is there and it is good.

What changes is the consumer. Those policies key off a session identity, the role running the query, which works when every human logs in as themselves.

An agent breaks that. One process serves everybody, and the identity that matters is whoever the agent is answering for, not the credential it connected with. Get it wrong once and a coworker's Gmail turns up in an answer, with no dashboard boundary to catch it on the way out.

So every read carries an explicit scope instead of inheriting one from the connection. Org scoping, per-connection visibility, and per-resource membership all become part of the SQL that runs. A connection backed by a personal OAuth login is forced private by a database trigger. When a membership sync goes stale the gate fails closed, so a stalled sync hides data rather than leaking it.

None of this is beyond a warehouse. Bind a request-scoped identity, let engine-level policies do the work, and you have built the same thing the right way. What a warehouse gives you is permission to defer it, because a missing policy usually shows up as a dashboard nobody can open. An agent turns that same gap into a fluent sentence containing someone else's data. So the scope has to be mandatory on every read, not something you add when the compliance review lands.

## You cannot re-run a Behavior

The closest thing we have to a dbt model is a Behavior: a declared unit of work that runs on a cadence, reads the log, and writes derived events back. Underneath, a tick enqueues a row on a job queue, and that row moves through pending, claimed, and running, with heartbeat-based reaping when a worker dies. If you have configured a Snowflake Task or an Airflow DAG, you know this shape already.

The familiarity stops there.

Re-running a dbt model is usually cheap and usually safe. Not always: incremental models and snapshots carry state, sources move underneath you, and a full refresh on a large table costs real money. But the worst case is a wrong table or a bigger bill, which is why the ecosystem can treat re-running as the default recovery. Something looks off, you run it again.

A Behavior takes actions in systems we do not own. It sends the email. No `--full-refresh` unsends it, and no amount of compute buys the message back.

That one property is why everything around it looks stricter than a warehouse's scheduler. A run is claimed rather than merely scheduled. The claim query only ever selects work a human already approved. An approval is a durable event rather than a flag somebody flips in a UI. The orchestration is heavier because a failed run is not a stale table.

## What the warehouse still does better

If your question is analytical, the warehouse wins and it is not close. Columnar storage and decades of query optimization beat a Postgres event log at scanning a billion rows for one aggregate, and the dbt ecosystem around it is better than anything we would build. We do not compete there. Metrics that need the warehouse read the warehouse, live, over a connector, and the answer gets composed rather than copied.

So the claim is narrower than replacing anything. Agent memory should borrow warehouse practice for ingestion, modelling, and provenance, because that work is done and it is good. What it cannot borrow is the shape. The loop has to close. Derived state stays a cache. The scope travels with the read. The transform is unsafe to repeat.

None of those four come from AI being special. They come from having a reader that acts on what it finds, in systems nobody here owns.

Your systems still own the truth. This store keeps what was observed, who is allowed to see it, and what every agent did about it.

Start with the [docs](/getting-started/), or read how the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/) works.

result.output:
1:Intelligence stopped being the blocker. Kimi K3 put 2.8 trillion parameters of open weights on Hugging Face this month. GLM 5.2 sits at the top of the coding arenas at a fraction of frontier pricing. DeepSeek V4 takes a million tokens of context. Any of them is smart enough for the work most companies actually want done, and if none of them are, a frontier lab ships something in six weeks.
3:What stops the agent you want to deploy is context. The model does not know your customers, your pricing exceptions, or which of two contradictory Slack messages is the current one.
5:Most agents answer that with a filesystem. [ChatGPT keeps a running summary of you across chats](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8590148-memory-faq), Anthropic's [memory tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool) is literally a directory the model reads and writes between sessions, and coding agents keep a repo of markdown under [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/). For one person that is the right answer and I would not replace it. It gives you no schema, though. Nothing stops two files from disagreeing about a customer's plan, nothing marks which one is current, and nothing records who wrote either. That is an analyst working on one laptop. It works at one desk, and nobody runs a company off it.
7:Companies solved this once already, by putting a warehouse in the middle and making it the thing everyone reads. I have argued that analogy in full in [The Operational Data Stack for Agents](/blog/the-operational-data-stack-for-agents/), and the split between the notebook and the warehouse in [Filesystem vs Database for Agent Memory](/blog/filesystem-vs-database-agent-memory/). This post is about what the storage underneath has to guarantee, because an agent only improves when its past is queryable. Retraining, a rewritten prompt, an eval set: each one needs a record of what the agent did, what a human said about it, and what happened next.
9:So Lobu's memory layer is closer to git than to a memory API. Every write is an append. Nothing is edited in place. Correcting a fact means writing a new one that points at the fact it replaces. History is walkable, provenance is a column, and human review is a merge that happens before the write lands rather than a cleanup afterwards.
11:The log is not another system of record. Slack owns the conversation, Stripe owns the payment, the warehouse owns revenue, and mirroring them into a second authority buys you a reconciliation problem you did not have. Our log is a proxy: an append-only record of observations about systems we do not own. The sources stay authoritative for the facts. The log is authoritative for what we observed, when, and what every agent did about it.
13:<TruthProxyDiagram />
15:## A memory write is a commit
17:The agent-facing surface is one MCP tool, [`save_memory`](/getting-started/memory/), and its contract is the whole model in a sentence: storage is append-only, pass `supersedes_event_id` to replace an existing fact, and the old event is hidden from future searches without losing history.
19:Agents are told to use it that way. The guidance we ship reads: "When a message changes a fact you already stored (an updated preference, status, count, location, or plan), first search for the prior memory to get its id, then save the new value with `supersedes_event_id` set to that id."
21:The chain is enforced, not conventional. A partial unique index means at most one event can supersede a given target, so the loser of a concurrent-supersede race gets a `23505` and a real error instead of a fork. Current state is a view over that: an event is current if nothing supersedes it. Read a fact's history and the server walks the `supersedes_event_id` linked list in both directions and hands back every version.
23:The workspace Lobu runs its own company on holds roughly 230,000 events, about 27,000 of which replace an earlier observation. You keep every version, and most of them nobody will ever read. That sounds wasteful right up until somebody asks what the agent believed on Tuesday.
25:## Ingestion is incremental by construction
27:Facts arrive through feeds. A feed is one [connector](/sdks/connectors/)-defined sync against one connection, and it carries a `checkpoint` that the connector advances itself, so the next run pulls from where the last one stopped rather than re-reading the source.
29:Duplicates are handled at the insert, not by the connector. Ingest dedupes on `(connection_id, origin_id)` under a per-item advisory lock, so two concurrent syncs of the same Slack thread serialize on that item and different items never contend. Re-running a sync is cheap and safe, which is the property that lets a connector be dumb.
31:Behaviors get incrementality from the log itself. A Behavior's unprocessed work is computed as a diff: total events per month, minus events already linked to one of that Behavior's completed windows. There is no cursor to corrupt and no watermark to reset. If a window fails, its events are simply still unlinked, so the next run picks them up.
33:## Behaviors are mutations on your data model
35:A [Behavior](/getting-started/behaviors/) is a trigger, a prompt, and optional named SQL sources over the events log. The trigger says when. The prompt says what matters. The sources are how it reads what a connector wrote, and a typed [reaction](/sdks/reactions/) is where it acts. It subscribes to company events, and when it runs it completes a window that records exactly which events it consumed.
37:What it produces goes back into the same graph in one of two shapes. It appends events, which is a memory, a summary, a notification, an approval request. Or it changes entities, which is the structured layer: a company's stage, a member's role, a deal's amount. That is the whole vocabulary. A Behavior is a mutation against your data model with a model in the middle deciding the arguments.
39:>
41:That loop needs one guard, and we learned it the mechanical way. Behaviors with no explicit source used to read every event. The server's own bookkeeping rows, `semantic_type` of `change` and `audit`, were invisible only by accident, because they were inserted with a null `occurred_at`. The moment we started stamping that column, a Behavior's own audit trail became new workspace content it would react to. The default source now excludes those two semantic types, and a migration rewrote the existing rows matched by exact literal so hand-authored sources were never touched.
43:## The human review step is a merge
45:Entity fields carry ownership. `entities.field_controls` is a sparse map where a key being present means a human owns that field. There is one write path for both humans and agents, and it behaves differently by source: a human write sets the value and marks it owned, and an agent write only lands on fields no human has claimed.
47:Blocked fields do not fail silently and they do not overwrite. Every user-facing entity mutation runs through a gate that can allow, deny, or defer, and a deferred write becomes a pending run plus an approval event, queued strictly after the caller's transaction commits so approvals never ride a write that might roll back.
49:The approval event is what makes this collaboration rather than a yes/no vote. Alongside the proposed input, the event carries the JSON schema describing that input, so the web app renders a form and the reviewer edits the arguments before approving. One run that proposed twenty field changes groups into one card through its window id. The same event renders as a Slack card with buttons, and both paths call the same tool underneath. Which actions need a human at all is [operator configuration](/guides/tool-policy/), not something the agent decides.
51:>
53:Rejection is not a dead end either. A correction a human makes on a Behavior's output is itself an event, `semantic_type` of `correction`, and the next run of that Behavior gets the most recent correction per field folded into its prompt. Superseded corrections are dropped so the prompt does not accumulate the whole argument. The human is editing the agent's future behaviour by editing the record, which is the only feedback channel we have that survives a model swap.
55:## Every run writes to the same log
57:Agents still get a filesystem. Each conversation gets a [workspace](/getting-started/architecture/) for the scratch work: downloaded PDFs, intermediate CSVs, generated reports. That layer stays ephemeral on purpose. What leaves it is the write to the log, and every one of those names the run that made it. A run carries the Behavior that fired it, the agent that Behavior belongs to, and the user who initiated it if a human did. Roughly 90,000 of those 230,000 events name their run.
59:The same is true of agents we do not run. Connect ChatGPT to the [Lobu MCP server](/guides/mcp-proxy/) and every tool call it makes writes an audit event carrying the agent id, the MCP session, the client, and the calling user, alongside the tool name, a hash of the arguments, and a redacted preview. The audit records the call's shape, never its content, and credentials are consumed to the end of the value rather than to the first space. On Slack, a thread is a conversation in its own right, keyed as `slack:{channel}:{thread}` and pinned to one agent, so a thread is a durable run rather than a session that dies with the socket.
61:>
63:That is what gives you one audit trail across managed and external agents instead of one per vendor. "Why does this company say Series B" resolves to a run, a window, the events that window consumed, and the human who approved the promotion.
65:## Where the analogy stops
67:There is no force-push and no rebase, because a fact we mirrored can change under us and the honest record of that is a new observation pointing at the old one. There is no revert either. You cannot un-send the email. That asymmetry is the reason the gate sits before the write and the correction is an append.
69:None of this is clever, which is the part I would defend. The model in the loop gets better a few times a year when a lab ships something, and that has stopped being the interesting variable. The record underneath gets better every week.
71:Start with the [memory layer](/getting-started/memory/), or read how [Behaviors](/getting-started/behaviors/) are defined.

content.text:
Both posts rewritten. PR #36: https://github.com/lobu-ai/landing/pull/36 — dev server on 4321 has it live now.

You were right that it was a pattern, not a sentence. Name something the old system doesn't do, answer it with a short clause about ours. It was carrying two of the four section headings and most of the section closers:

- `## A warehouse is terminal. This one writes back.` → `## Writing the decision back`
- `## Warehouses do not ask who is asking. This one has to.` → `## Every read has to carry who it is for`
- `## Derived state, not staged tiers` → `## Everything downstream is only a cache`
- `## The transform is not idempotent` → `## You cannot re-run a Behavior`

Plus closers like "That is the difference between a system that reports and a system that improves" — cut, because the paragraph above it already said that.

The other half was jargon that was never doing work. The densest one:

**Was**
> The chain is enforced, not conventional. A partial unique index means at most one event can supersede a given target, so the loser of a concurrent-supersede race gets a `23505` and a real error instead of a fork. Current state is a view over that: an event is current if nothing supersedes it.

**Now**
> None of this relies on the agent behaving. The database only lets one event replace a given fact, so if two agents try to replace the same one at the same moment, the second gets an error rather than quietly creating a second version of the truth.
>
> So "what is true right now" is not a field anyone maintains. A fact is current if nothing has replaced it. That is the whole rule.

Same claim, and the point now arrives before the mechanism instead of after it. Similar treatment for advisory locks, watermarks, `semantic_type`, and `field_controls`.

CDC and dbt stayed in the data-stack post. There the analogy *is* the argument, and the reader it's written for knows both words — de-jargoning that would blunt the thesis.

Length is basically unchanged: 1805 → 1752 and 1694 → 1634 words. It's not shorter, it's just less work to read.

I also closed the figure-versus-prose disagreement you'd been carrying: the post said whatever happens next "leaves the system," directly beneath a diagram that draws the return path. Actions do come back, as raw activity. The decision is what never does — sharper, and it agrees with the picture.

**The new cover is in, but it didn't pick up either of the two changes.** Headline still reads THE MODERN DATA STACK BUILT FOR AGENTS under a title that says Operational, and the sources column is still CRM / email / documents / databases / product with no warehouse. It also went 16:9 where the other covers are 3:2, so the blog index card crops it differently. If ChatGPT keeps dropping the headline edit, the reliable move is to ask for the title text verbatim rather than describing the change.

**Confidence: 88** on the rewrite — build green, every replacement asserted on exact match so nothing applied silently, and I grepped both files for surviving antithesis constructions and em dashes (zero in prose; two in alt text). The 12% is that voice is your call, not something I can verify.

2. Regenerate the cover with the headline text given verbatim, plus a warehouse in the sources column.

content.text:
Honestly? I think the retitle was a mistake, and I'd go back.

"Operational Data Stack" is a coined category. "Modern data stack" is a term people already use and search; "operational data stack" is one you'd be introducing in the title and then spending the post earning. Inventing a category name is a marketing move, and it's the same register you just had me strip out of the prose.

It also spoils the turn. The post's structure is: take the familiar analogy seriously, most of it transfers, now here are the four places it breaks. That only works if the title hands the reader the familiar thing. Put the correction in the title and the first half reads like throat-clearing before the real point.

And the practical bit: the art says MODERN. Right now that's a live inconsistency I flagged as needing a regeneration. Reverting deletes that problem instead of paying to fix it.

One more thing worth knowing — I just checked prod, and the old URL `lobu.ai/blog/the-modern-data-stack-for-agents/` is *still* returning 200 off Cloudflare's cache. It hasn't gone cold yet. If we revert now, nobody ever hits a dead link. Wait a few hours and that stops being true.

Your instinct in the question is the right one, by the way — keep "modern data stack," add what changes. The phrasing just needs work. "The Modern Data Stack Is Operational With Agents" is a mouthful and buries the subject.

So: revert to **The Modern Data Stack for Agents**, and if you want the turn visible up front, put it in the description rather than the title — that's what shows under the headline on the index and in the unfurl. Something like "Most of the analogy transfers. It breaks in four places."

If you'd rather the title carry it, the version I'd defend is **The Modern Data Stack for Agents, and Where It Breaks** — keeps the search term, states the payload, invents nothing.

The valid part of the original criticism was that the title over-promises a replacement. That's real, but the fix is the first paragraph and the description, not renaming the category.

Say the word and I'll fold the revert into #36 — it's one frontmatter line, one filename, and one inbound link, and it makes the cover art correct for free.
